prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms are interrogated at a magic wavelength, opening the regime of fractional frequency uncertainty near 1e-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: Katori and Ye for optical lattice clocks. After the first round I tested it against the chair's question on separation from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. The 2005 prize rewarded the frequency comb as a tool that links optical and microwave frequencies, and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single trapped quantum systems, with ion clocks as a showcase. Neither covers the idea that makes lattice clocks distinct: choosing a magic wavelength so that a lattice can hold many neutral atoms at once without shifting the clock transition, which brings the statistical advantage of large ensembles together with the absence of Doppler and recoil effects. That idea, and its demonstration and refinement to about 1e-18 accuracy and record stability, is a separate achievement in kind. It also has the strongest verification on the shortlist, because independent lattice clocks, and ion clocks, are compared directly and agree at the 1e-18 level. The consequences are concrete: tests of constants and relativistic time dilation at the millimetre to centimetre scale, clock-based geodesy, and a real prospect of a redefined second. The two-name credit follows two identifiable contributions, concept and first demonstrations (Katori) against accuracy, stability and many-body control (Ye), and stays inside the three-person limit.
statement.case_against: The overlap with earlier metrology prizes remains the main risk, and the citation has to carry the burden of stating what is new relative to 2005 and 2012. Danielsson's point that the discovery content is thinner than for a new class of matter is a fair one and I have not fully answered it; I can only say that a new regime of measurement is itself a discovery for this prize. Priority for the magic-wavelength proposal and the claims of other neutral-atom and ion-clock groups still rest on recollection, not on documents in the shortlist. B009 has the broadest support, and I cannot treat a count of three supporters against six as irrelevant, even though a count is not a scientific argument. If B009 goes forward, its credit gap around Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Hasan is real and cannot be repaired by the three-name limit.

responses.point: Olsson holds that B009 is not incremental after 2016, because that prize covered topological phase transitions and phases in model systems while B009 showed that band structure of real insulators carries a topological invariant with protected edge states, observed in real crystals.
responses.response: That distinction is persuasive and I withdraw most of my incrementalism objection. The 2016 prize concerned topological order in model systems, and Kane-Mele with the HgTe experiment is a different step, since it ties a Z2 invariant to measurable edge transport in real materials. My residual concern is credit, not novelty. You and Danielsson both say the BHZ proposal and Hasan's work cannot be fitted into the trio, and I do not think a citation that names prediction plus first realisation removes that problem. I turn your own argument for B009 around: the same test of overlap that you apply to B026 against the comb and ion-clock prizes is, for B026, answered by a specific physical idea, the magic wavelength, and I think that is at least as separable as the band-topology step.

responses.point: Mehlig asks whether I see clocks as outranking a field that changed how condensed-matter theory classifies phases, and notes that support for B026 is narrow and that B009 has a coherent theory-plus-experiment structure.
responses.response: I do not claim that clocks outrank topological insulators in conceptual reach, and I accept that B009 changed how a whole community thinks. I do not rank by breadth of influence alone, though. The prize is for a discovery or invention whose attribution can be stated precisely, and on that criterion B026 is cleaner, with two names mapping onto two steps and nobody essential left out of a named trio. You rightly note that the support is narrow, three of eight in the opening and two in round 1. I take that as a reason to listen to the six, not as a reason to change my own judgment. If the committee concludes that the BHZ and Hasan omissions are acceptable with an open citation, then I regard B009 as a fully respectable outcome and would not oppose it. I am not changing my preferred configuration, but I rank the gap between B026 and B009 as small.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B026 sixth because its significance lies mainly in measurement capability, with thinner discovery content, and would accept it only as a second part of a two-achievement prize if topological insulators were not available.
responses.response: I think the discovery content in B026 is more than capability. The magic-wavelength lattice was a new physical idea, and the regime it opened, with many-body interactions and quantum-engineered interrogation of a lattice clock, produced new physics about collective shifts and correlations. I agree that a pairing with B009 is not feasible at the available name count, since B009 already uses three names and B026 uses two, which exceeds the limit of three people. That is another reason I regard this as a choice between single achievements, not a negotiation.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that independent lattice clocks now agree with each other and with ion clocks at 1e-18, which is what makes a redefinition of the second a real prospect, and that B037 should not dilute the metrological story.
responses.response: I agree with the verification argument and have used it above. On B037, I keep it as an alternative because it is a mature platform with a well-defined experimental trio, but I accept your point that it is a different kind of achievement and I do not regard it as a second part for this year. I also note that neither of us can verify the magic-wavelength priority from the materials, so the citation should name the idea and the demonstrated performance without assigning priority further than the two credited names support.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as a distinct achievement from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which depends on how well the citation states the role of the magic wavelength and many-atom interrogation.
Priority for the magic-wavelength proposal and the contributions of other neutral-atom and ion-clock groups are not verified from the materials and rest on recollection.
Whether the committee should accept the BHZ and Hasan omissions in B009, given six members who prefer it; if so, I would not oppose it.
Whether my Boulder research stay and field proximity should lead me to recuse myself on B026.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. My profile documents a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my doctoral period. Hall's comb work is the 2005 prize, which is part of the history of B026 and of the group around Jun Ye. I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye and no documented tie to any credited name in B009 or B037. I am an atomic physicist in the same broad field (Lund Quantum Information Group, laser spectroscopy). My earlier WACQT management role is relevant to B010 only, which is not in my preferred configuration. I leave it to the committee to decide whether the Boulder connection requires recusal on B026; if it is so decided I would not take part in a vote between B026 and other candidates.
